title: The Armenian genocide (1915)
hook: Armenians, an old Christian people, are deported and killed under the Ottoman government; told carefully and honestly

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stille Nacht sung across the trenches during the Christmas truce. Your line was silent night in no man's land. What did you hand across, and what came back? Day nine hundred forty-six.

A priest sits at a table with a notebook, writing down a song an old woman in a mountain village has just sung for him. A work song, sung while plowing. He's been walking from village to village, saving tunes that were never written down. His name is Komitas. He's an Armenian priest and a composer, and these songs are his people's memory. Then one night, during the First World War, he is arrested in Constantinople along with other Armenian leaders, writers and clergy. Some of them never come back. Today is a hard day in the story, and we'll go slowly.

The Armenians are an old Christian people, with their own church, their own alphabet and their own hymns, living in the lands of the Ottoman Empire. During the First World War, the Ottoman government arrested Armenian leaders, then forced whole Armenian communities from their homes. Men were often killed near their towns. Women, children and the old were marched toward the Syrian desert, and huge numbers died on the way, of killing, hunger, thirst and exhaustion. Assyrian and Greek Christians suffered in those years too. Historians who study these years, the Armenian churches, and the title of today's lesson call it genocide: an attempt to destroy a people. The government of Turkey disputes that word. Here we tell it as survivors and historians have recorded it, and we name that dispute rather than hide it. Two more true things belong in the telling. Survivors' accounts describe Turkish, Kurdish and Arab neighbors, Muslims, who hid Armenian families or took in orphans, sometimes at risk to themselves. And Komitas survived the arrests, but the horror broke him, and he never composed again. The songs he saved are still sung. There is a line in the Gospel of Matthew, about the children killed at Bethlehem, quoted from the prophet Jeremiah: "Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." The Bible doesn't hurry past grief like that. It lets it stand. The Armenian Apostolic Church has named the victims martyrs and saints, and Armenian communities gather each spring to remember them. And on a cross, a dying thief once asked for the same thing: "Lord, remember me." Remembering isn't revenge. It's refusing to let people disappear.

Here's the practice: learn one Armenian name. Today, it's Komitas. Settle, and breathe. Say the name quietly: Komitas. A priest who walked mountain villages saving songs, and lost his own voice to grief. Picture the old woman singing to him while he writes. Then let your mind widen to the families on the roads, whose names you don't know. You don't have to feel anything in particular. Just hold them. If you pray, you can ask God to remember them. If you don't, let the name Komitas stand for all of them for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Komitas. The Armenian priest and composer who saved his people's songs, was broken by the arrests of 1915, and never composed again.
Your line: remember them. Today, tell one person the name Komitas and one true thing about him, so that the name travels a little farther. Day nine hundred forty-six.

notes: Sensitive day. Claims rule: the index hook's 'over a million' and 'most of them Christians' are cut (no counts); the voice says 'huge numbers died'. Commonly cited estimates are roughly 600,000 to 1.5 million; a scholar should decide whether any figure belongs here. Suggest updating the outline hook.

Responsibility is placed on 'the Ottoman government'; Turks and Muslims as a people are not blamed, and Muslim rescuers are named. Check tone with an Armenian Christian reviewer and a Muslim reviewer.
'The government of Turkey disputes that word' is stated as current fact; confirm wording is fair and accurate.

Komitas: priest-composer who collected village songs; arrested with Armenian intellectuals in Constantinople (24 April 1915); survived, never recovered, never composed again. 'Some of them never come back' about those arrested (most were killed): confirm wording.
'Men were often killed near their towns', death marches toward the Syrian desert: confirm.
'Assyrian and Greek Christians suffered in those years too': confirm phrasing.
Canonization of the victims by the Armenian Apostolic Church (2015) and the annual remembrance in spring (24 April): dates omitted; confirm.
'Living in the lands of the Ottoman Empire' simplifies a longer history in Anatolia; confirm.
Original is null: no Greek or Hebrew word fits better than the Armenian names; a Keeper may want an Armenian-script word.
Editor pass: cut the general claim that churches read Matthew 2:18 'when children are killed'; the line is now tied to its own setting in Matthew.
Second editor pass: rewrote the garbled 'say plainly that this is contested by the state' line so the Turkish government's dispute is named once, plainly.

Audit: 'Here we tell what Armenians remember' made a documented history sound like one community's memory set against a state's denial. Now: historians who study these years and the Armenian churches call it genocide; told 'as survivors and historians have recorded it'. A Keeper and historian should confirm the wording.
